# Limine configuration file

## Location of the config file

Limine scans for the config file on *the boot drive*. On EFI, the volume
containing the EFI executable of the booted Limine is scanned first. The
drive is then scanned as a whole, followed by every partition sequentially -
first partition first, last partition last. On each volume the candidates are
tried in this order: on EFI, `<EFI app path>/limine.conf` first, or
`/EFI/BOOT/limine.conf` where that path cannot be determined; then
`/boot/limine/limine.conf`, `/boot/limine.conf`, `/limine/limine.conf`, and
`/limine.conf`.

These names are matched case insensitively; see [Paths](#paths) for how paths
elsewhere in the config file are matched.

Once the file is located, Limine will use it as its config file. Other possible
candidates in subsequent partitions or directories are ignored.

It is thus imperative that the intended config file is placed in a location
that will not be shadowed by another candidate config file.

On EFI, should Limine fail to determine which volume it was booted from, it
reports the condition as a bug and waits for a keypress. It then scans every
volume it can see, for `/EFI/limine/limine.conf` and `/EFI/BOOT/limine.conf`
before the four names above.

### Config via SMBIOS

Alternatively, if present, Limine considers first and foremost configurations
supplied to it as SMBIOS OEM String entries (Type 11). Such configurations are
accepted if the first string of such an entry starts with the prefix of
`limine:config:`. The rest of the string is taken as the config file. If such a
configuration is found, no further scanning for config files is done. As such,
in this SMBIOS-provided config file scenario, the `boot():` drive is undefined
on BIOS, and set to the boot device of Limine on UEFI.

## Structure of the config file

The Limine configuration file is comprised of *menu entries* and *options*.
Comments begin in '#' and can only be on their own lines.

### Menu entries and sub-entries

*Menu entries* describe *entries* which the user can select in the *boot menu*.

A *menu entry* is opened by a line starting with `/` followed by a
newline-terminated string, that being the title of the entry which the user
will see.
Any *local option* that comes after it, and before another *menu entry*, or
the end of the file, will be part of that *menu entry*.

A *menu entry* can be a directory, meaning it can hold sub-entries. In order
for an entry to become a directory, it needs to have a sub-entry following
right after it.
(A `comment` option may be present between the beginning of the directory entry
and the beginning of the sub-entry).

A *sub-entry* is a menu entry started with a number of `/` greater than 1
prepended to it.
Each `/` represents 1 level deeper down the tree hierarchy of directories and
entries.

Directories can be expanded (meaning they will not show up as collapsed in the
menu) by default if a `+` is put between the `/`s and the beginning of the
entry's title.

### Options

*Options* are simple `option_name: string...` style "assignments".
The string can have spaces and other special characters, without requiring
quotations. New lines are delimiters. Option names are not case sensitive.
An option's value is truncated at 4095 characters.

Some *options* are part of an entry (*local*), some other options are *global*.
*Global options* can appear anywhere in the file and are not part of an entry,
although usually one would put them at the beginning of the config.
Some *local options* work the same between entries using any *protocol*, while
other *local options* are specific to a given *protocol*.

Some options take *paths* as strings; these are described in the next section.

*Global options* are:

Miscellaneous:

* `timeout` - Specifies the timeout in seconds before the selected *entry* is
  automatically booted (see `default_entry` option). Decimal values such as
  `0.25` are accepted, and the timeout is capped at `9999` seconds. If set to
  `no`, disable automatic boot. If set to `0`, boot the selected entry
  instantly, without showing the menu. A value that is neither `no` nor a
  number is treated as `0`. On UEFI, the Boot Loader Interface's
  `LoaderConfigTimeoutOneShot` EFI variable, where set (for example by
  `systemctl reboot --boot-loader-menu=`), overrides this option for the boot
  that consumes it, and the persistent `LoaderConfigTimeout` variable (for
  example from `bootctl set-timeout`) is honoured only where this option is
  not set.
* `quiet` - If set to `yes`, enable quiet mode, where all screen output except
  panics and important warnings is suppressed. If `timeout` is neither `0` nor
  `no`, the `timeout` still occurs, and pressing any key during the timeout
  will reveal the menu and disable quiet mode. Where automatic boot is
  disabled, the menu is shown regardless.
* `serial` - If set to `yes`, enable serial I/O for the bootloader.
* `serial_baudrate` - If `serial` is set to `yes`, this specifies the baudrate
  to use for serial I/O. Defaults to `115200`, which is also the maximum. The
  minimum is `50`, and the rate must divide `115200` exactly, which every
  standard rate in that range does except `110`, `2000` and `56000`; any other
  value is treated as `115200`. BIOS only, ignored with Limine UEFI.
* `global_dtb` - If set, use this DTB instead of the firmware-provided DTB for
  Limine itself, as well as for any booted entry whose protocol supports DTBs
  and the DTB is not locally overridden with `dtb_path`.
* `default_entry` - Entry which will be automatically selected at startup.
  Can be a 1-based entry index (e.g. `1`), or an entry path (e.g.
  `OSes/Arch Linux`). Entry paths use `/` as a directory separator; literal
  `/`, `\`, and `#` characters in entry names must be escaped as `\/`, `\\`,
  and `\#` respectively. If multiple sibling entries share the same name, append
  `#N` to select the Nth duplicate (e.g. `Arch Linux#1` for the second entry
  named `Arch Linux`). If unspecified, it is `1`. On UEFI, a Boot Loader
  Interface `LoaderEntryOneShot` request takes precedence over this option, and
  so does `remember_last_entry` where it has an entry to restore. The
  persistent `LoaderEntryDefault` variable is consulted only where this option
  is not set. A value that does not name a bootable entry still counts as set,
  but disables autoboot (and shows the menu if `timeout` is `0` and/or `quiet`
  is `yes`): that covers a path or index matching nothing, and a path or index
  naming a directory.
* `remember_last_entry` - If set to `yes`, remember last booted entry. Takes
  precedence over `default_entry` and over the persistent `LoaderEntryDefault`
  variable; `default_entry` applies only where this option is `no` or no
  remembered entry resolves. (UEFI only).
* `graphics` - If set to `no`, force text mode for the boot menu, else use
  a video mode.
* `wallpaper` - Path to a file to use as a wallpaper. BMP, PNG, JPEG, and QOI
  formats are supported. There can be multiple of this option, in which case
  the wallpaper will be randomly selected from the provided options.
* `wallpaper_style` - The style which will be used to display the wallpaper
  image: `tiled`, `centered`, or `stretched`. Default is `stretched`.
* `backdrop` - When the background style is `centered`, this specifies the
  colour of the backdrop for parts of the screen not covered by the background
  image, in RRGGBB format.
* `verbose` - If set to `yes`, print additional information during boot.
  Defaults to not verbose.
* `terse` - If set to `yes`, suppress informational loading messages (such as
  "Loading kernel" and "Loading module") when booting any entry. The menu and
  any error or panic messages remain unaffected. Defaults to `no`.
* `randomise_memory` - If set to `yes`, randomise the contents of RAM at bootup
  in order to find bugs related to non zeroed memory or for security reasons.
  This option will slow down boot time significantly. In the case of IA-32,
  BIOS or UEFI, this will only randomise memory below 4GiB.
* `randomize_memory` - Alias of `randomise_memory`.
* `hash_mismatch_panic` - If set to `no`, do not panic if there is a hash
  mismatch for a file. A warning is printed and Limine then waits for a
  keypress: `Y` continues the boot, any other key returns to the menu. Forced
  to `yes` when Secure Boot is active and a config hash is enrolled.
* `measured_boot` - If set to `yes`, opt in to measured boot. Forced to `yes`
  when Secure Boot is active and a config hash is enrolled, and forced back to
  `no` if the firmware does not expose a TPM 2.0/CC measurement interface. See
  [USAGE.md](USAGE.md#measured-boot).
* `firmware_logo` - If set to `yes`, restore the OEM firmware boot logo upon
  handoff to the OS, instead of leaving a blank screen, by clearing the
  "displayed" status bit in the ACPI BGRT table so the OS redraws the logo
  itself. The image is re-centred for the active resolution. UEFI only;
  defaults to `no`.
* `keyboard_layout` - Specifies a keyboard layout to remap printable
  keystrokes to before they reach the menu and editor. Currently only
  `dvorak` and `azerty` are supported. If unset, no remapping is applied
  and keystrokes are used as-is. This assumes the underlying firmware
  resolves keystrokes as US-QWERTY; on firmware/keyboard combinations that
  already resolve a different layout natively, this option may produce
  incorrect output.
* `mouse` - If set to `no`, disable mouse support in the boot menu. Defaults
  to `yes`, in which case, if a mouse is present, the menu selection follows
  the pointer, left clicking an entry boots it (or expands a directory), and
  the scroll wheel moves the selection. Using the mouse stops the `timeout`
  countdown, as pressing a key does. On BIOS this uses the PS/2 (or emulated
  PS/2) mouse; on UEFI any pointer device the firmware exposes.

Limine interface control options:

* `interface_resolution` - Specify screen resolution to be used by the Limine
  interface (menu, editor, console...) in the form `<width>x<height>`. This
  will *only* affect the Limine interface, not any booted OS. If not specified,
  Limine will pick a resolution automatically. If the resolution is not
  available, Limine will pick another one automatically. Ignored if using text
  mode.
* `interface_rotation` - Specifies the rotation of the Limine interface.
  It can be any of the following values: `0`, `90`, `180`, `270`. Default is `0`.
* `interface_branding` - A string that will be displayed on top of the Limine
  interface.
* `interface_branding_colour` - An `RRGGBB` hexadecimal value specifying the
  colour of the branding string. Default is `00aaaa`.
* `interface_branding_color` - Alias of `interface_branding_colour`.
* `interface_help_hidden` - Hides the help text located at the top of the
  screen showing the key bindings.
* `interface_help_colour` - An `RRGGBB` hexadecimal value specifying the
  colour of the help strings. Default is `00aa00`.
* `interface_help_color` - Alias of `interface_help_colour`.
* `interface_help_colour_bright` - An `RRGGBB` hexadecimal value specifying
  the brighter accent colour used for the auto-boot countdown digit. If
  unspecified, it is derived from `interface_help_colour` by adding `0x55`
  to each channel (saturating at `0xff`).
* `interface_help_color_bright` - Alias of `interface_help_colour_bright`.

Limine graphical terminal control options:

These are ignored if using text mode.

* `term_font` - Path to a font file to be used instead of the default one for
  the menu and terminal. The font file must be a code page 437 character set
  comprised of 256 consecutive glyph bitmaps. Each glyph's bitmap must be
  expressed left to right (1 byte per row), and top to bottom (16 bytes per
  whole glyph by default; see `term_font_size`). See e.g. the
  [VGA text mode font](https://github.com/viler-int10h/vga-text-mode-fonts)
  collection for fonts.
* `term_font_size` - The size of each glyph of the font in dots, which must
  correspond to the font file, or display will be garbled or loading issues
  will occur. All fonts are assumed to be of width 8, so the first value of
  the pair (AKA the `8` in `8x16`) must be `8`; any other width is refused and
  the default font is used in place of `term_font`. To set horizontal spacing
  between glyphs on screen, see `term_font_spacing`. Defaults to `8x16`.
  Ignored if `term_font` not set or if the font fails to load.
* `term_font_scale` - Scaling for the font in the x and y directions. `2x2`
  would display the font in double size, which is useful on high-DPI displays
  at native resolution. `2x1` only makes the font twice as wide, similar to the
  VGA 40 column mode. `4x2` might be good for a narrow font on a high
  resolution display. Each factor must be between 1 and 8; any value that is not
  such a pair is treated as if the option were unset. If unset, the scaling
  follows the resolution: `1x1` below 2560x1440, `2x2` from there, and `4x4`
  from 5120x2880.
* `term_font_spacing` - Horizontal spacing, in pixels, between glyphs on
  screen. Also applies to the built-in Limine font. Defaults to 1. 0 is
  allowed; a value above 8, or one that is not a number, is treated as if the
  option were unset.
* `term_palette` - Specifies the colour palette used by the terminal (RRGGBB).
  It is a `;` separated array of 8 colours: black, red, green, brown, blue,
  magenta, cyan, and gray. Ignored if not using a graphical terminal.
* `term_palette_bright` - Specifies the bright colour palette used by the
  terminal (RRGGBB). It is a `;` separated array of 8 bright colours:
  dark gray, bright red, bright green, yellow, bright blue, bright magenta,
  bright cyan, and white. Ignored if not using a graphical terminal.
* `term_background` - Terminal text background colour (TTRRGGBB). TT stands for
  transparency. Defaults to `00000000`, or to `80000000` when a `wallpaper` is
  displayed.
* `term_foreground` - Terminal text foreground colour (RRGGBB).
* `term_background_bright` - Terminal text background bright colour (RRGGBB).
* `term_foreground_bright` - Terminal text foreground bright colour (RRGGBB).
* `term_margin` - Set the amount of margin, in pixels, around the terminal.
  Defaults to `0`, or to `64` when a `wallpaper` is displayed.
* `term_margin_gradient` - Set the thickness in pixel for the gradient around
  the terminal. Clamped to `term_margin`. Defaults to `0`, or to `4` when a
  `wallpaper` is displayed.

Editor control options:

* `editor_enabled` - If set to `no`, the editor will not be accessible.
  Defaults to `yes` unless a config hash is enrolled. Unconditionally
  disabled when Secure Boot is active and a config hash is enrolled.
* `editor_highlighting` - If set to `no`, syntax highlighting in the editor
  will be disabled. Defaults to `yes`.
* `editor_validation` - If set to `no`, the editor will not alert you about
  invalid options or syntax errors. Defaults to `yes`.

*Locally assignable (non protocol specific) options* are:

* `comment` - An optional comment string that will be displayed by the
  bootloader on the menu when an entry is selected.
* `protocol` - The boot protocol that will be used to boot the
  kernel/executable. Valid protocols are: `linux`, `limine`, `multiboot`
  (or `multiboot1`), `multiboot2`, `efi`, `efi_boot_entry` and `bios`.
* `cmdline` - The command line string to be passed to the kernel/executable.
  Can be omitted.
* `kernel_cmdline` - Alias of `cmdline`.
* `if_fw_type` - Hide the entry if the firmware does not match. Valid values
  are: `BIOS`, `UEFI`
* `if_arch` - Hide the entry if the current CPU architecture is not in the
  space separated list of permitted architectures
    * see the `ARCH` macro in [Built-in macros](#built-in-macros) for a list of possible architectures
* `if_loader_arch` - Hide the entry if the Limine binary's own architecture is
  not in the space separated list of permitted architectures
    * see the `LOADER_ARCH` macro in [Built-in macros](#built-in-macros) for details

> **NOTE:** `uefi` and `efi_chainload` are aliases of the `efi` protocol
> option. `bios_chainload` is an alias of the `bios` protocol option.

> **NOTE:** BIOS chainloading entries will be hidden when booting using UEFI
> and vice-versa.

*Locally assignable (protocol specific) options* are:

* Linux protocol:
  * `path` - The path of the kernel.
  * `kernel_path` - Alias of `path`.
  * `module_path` - The path to a module (such as initramfs). This option can
    be specified multiple times to specify multiple modules.
  * `resolution` - The resolution to be used. This setting takes the form of
    `<width>x<height>x<bpp>`. If the resolution is not available, Limine will
    pick another one automatically. Omitting `<bpp>` will default to 32.
  * `textmode` - If set to `yes`, prefer text mode. (BIOS only)
  * `dtb_path` - A device tree blob to pass instead of the one provided by the
    firmware.

* Limine protocol:
  * `path` - The path of the executable.
  * `kernel_path` - Alias of `path`.
  * `module_path` - The path to a module. This option can be specified multiple
    times to specify multiple modules.
  * `module_string` - A string to be associated with a module. This option can
    also be specified multiple times. It applies to the module described by the
    last module option specified.
  * `module_cmdline` - Alias of `module_string`.
  * `resolution` - The resolution to be used. This setting takes the form of
    `<width>x<height>x<bpp>`. If the resolution is not available, Limine will
    pick another one automatically. Omitting `<bpp>` will default to 32.
  * `kaslr` - For relocatable executables, if set to `yes`, enable kernel
    address space layout randomisation. KASLR is disabled by default.
  * `randomise_hhdm_base` - If set to `yes`, randomise the base address of the
    higher half direct map. If set to `no`, do not. By default it is `yes` if
    KASLR is supported and enabled, else it is `no`.
  * `randomize_hhdm_base` - Alias of `randomise_hhdm_base`.
  * `max_paging_mode`, `min_paging_mode` - Limit the maximum and minimum paging
    modes to one of the following:
    - x86-64 and aarch64: `4level`, `5level`.
    - riscv64: `sv39`, `sv48`, `sv57`.
    - loongarch64: `4level`.
  * `paging_mode` - Equivalent to setting both `max_paging_mode` and
    `min_paging_mode` to the same value.
  * `dtb_path` - A device tree blob to pass instead of the one provided by the
    firmware.

* multiboot1 and multiboot2 protocols:
  * `path` - The path of the executable.
  * `kernel_path` - Alias of `path`.
  * `module_path` - The path to a module. This option can be specified multiple
    times to specify multiple modules.
  * `module_string` - A string to be passed to a module. This option can also
    be specified multiple times. It applies to the module described by the last
    module option specified.
  * `resolution` - The resolution to be used should the executable request a
    graphical framebuffer. This setting takes the form of
    `<width>x<height>x<bpp>` and *overrides* any resolution requested by the
    executable. If the resolution is not available, Limine will pick another
    one automatically. Omitting `<bpp>` will default to 32.
  * `textmode` - If set to `yes`, prefer text mode. (BIOS only)

* EFI Chainload protocol:
  * `path` - Path of the EFI application to chainload.
  * `image_path` - Alias of `path`.
  * `resolution` - The resolution to be used. This setting takes the form of
    `<width>x<height>x<bpp>`. If the resolution is not available, Limine will
    pick another one automatically. Omitting `<bpp>` will default to 32.

* EFI Boot Entry protocol:
  * `entry` - The name of the EFI boot entry to reboot into.

* BIOS Chainload protocol:
  * `drive` - The 1-based drive to chainload, if omitted, assume boot drive.
    Only hard disks can be chainloaded, so this is always a hard disk index;
    booted from optical media, an omitted `drive` therefore selects the hard
    disk of the same index rather than the boot medium.
  * `partition` - The 1-based partition to chainload, if omitted, or set to 0,
    chainload drive (MBR).
  * `mbr_id` - Optional. If passed, use an MBR ID (32-bit hex value) to
    identify the drive containing the volume to chainload. Overrides `drive`,
    if present, but does *not* override `partition`.
  * `gpt_uuid` or `gpt_guid` - Optional. If passed, use the GPT GUID to
    identify the drive containing the volume to chainload. Overrides `drive`
    and `mbr_id`, if present, but does *not* override `partition`.

  To boot FreeBSD on a BIOS/GPT disk, point `partition` at the `freebsd-boot`
  partition. Limine recognises it by its GPT type GUID and emulates FreeBSD's
  `pmbr`: it loads the whole partition (`gptboot`) and hands off to it, rather
  than treating it as a conventional boot record (which it is not, as it has no
  `0xAA55` signature).

## Paths

A Limine path is used to locate files in the whole system. It is comprised of
a *resource*, a *resource argument*, and a *path*. It takes the form of:
```
resource(argument):/path
```

The format for `argument` changes depending on the resource used.

A resource can be one of the following:
* `boot` - If booted off PXE this is an alias of `tftp`. Else the `argument` is
  the 1-based decimal value representing the partition on the boot drive
  (values of 5+ for MBR logical partitions). If omitted, the partition
  containing the configuration file on the boot drive is used.
  For example: `boot(2):/...` will use partition 2 of the boot drive and
  `boot():/...` will use the partition containing the config file on the boot
  drive.
* `hdd` - Hard disk drives. The `argument` takes the form of `drive:partition`;
  for example: `hdd(3:1):/...` would use hard drive 3, partition 1. Partitions
  and drives are both 1-based (partition values of 5+ for MBR logical
  partitions). Omitting the partition is possible;
  for example: `hdd(2:):/...`. Omitting the partition will access the entire
  volume instead of a specific partition (useful for unpartitioned media).
* `odd` - Optical disk drives (CDs/DVDs/...). The `argument` takes the form of
  `drive:partition`; for example: `odd(3:1):/...` would use optical drive 3,
  partition 1. Partitions and drives are both 1-based (partition values of 5+
  for MBR logical partitions). Omitting the partition is possible;
  for example: `odd(2:):/...`. Omitting the partition will access the entire
  volume instead of a specific partition (useful for unpartitioned media, which
  is often the case for optical media).
* `guid` - The `argument` takes the form of a GUID/UUID, such as
  `guid(736b5698-5ae1-4dff-be2c-ef8f44a61c52):/...`. The GUID is that of either
  a filesystem, when available, or a GPT partition GUID, when using GPT, in a
  unified namespace.
* `uuid` - Alias of `guid`.
* `fslabel` - The `argument` is the name of the filesystem label of a
  partition, or of a whole volume where the filesystem occupies the entire
  medium. FAT volume labels and ISO 9660 volume identifiers are both read, and
  are matched case insensitively.
* `tftp` - The `argument` is the IP address of the tftp server to load the file
  from. If the argument is left empty (`tftp():/...`) the file will be loaded
  from the server Limine booted from. This resource is only available when
  booting off PXE.

Paths are matched case sensitively, with two exceptions. On FAT volumes a name
that fits the 8.3 short form is matched case insensitively, the short name
being stored uppercase; a name too long for that form is matched case
sensitively. On ISO9660 volumes a name carrying no Rock Ridge extension is
matched case insensitively, ISO9660 names being uppercase. The search for the
config file itself is case insensitive on every filesystem. Note that Joliet
supplementary volume descriptors are not read, so on an ISO9660 volume a long
name is only available through Rock Ridge.

For MBR, the four primary partitions take the numbers 1 to 4 by the slot they
occupy, whether or not that slot is used, and logical partitions are numbered
from 5 upwards by counting along the extended partition's chain. Every entry
with a non-zero size takes a number, except an entry of an extended type --
of which only the first non-empty one is the link to the next EBR -- and one
in an EBR's last two slots that falls outside either the extended partition
or the extent the link that led to that EBR declared.

A path can optionally be suffixed with a blake2b hash for the referenced file,
by appending a pound character (`#`) followed by the blake2b hash.
E.g.: `boot():/somemodule.tar#ca6914d2...446b470a`.
When Secure Boot is active and a config hash is enrolled, all file paths
**must** have a hash appended or Limine will panic (except for wallpapers and
fonts, which are silently skipped instead, falling back to defaults). Without
an enrolled hash Limine treats Secure Boot as inactive; see
[USAGE.md](USAGE.md#secure-boot).

A gzip-compressed resource is indicated by inserting a dollar character (`$`)
before the resource string. This allows for transparent decompression. For
such resources, the hash covers the consumed compressed gzip member bytes,
not the decompressed data and not trailing bytes outside the consumed member.
The hash thus authenticates the on-disk payload bytes Limine uses.

## Macros

Macros are strings that can be arbitrarily assigned to represent other strings.
For example:
```
${MY_MACRO}=Some text
```

Now, whenever `${MY_MACRO}` is used in the config file (except for an
assignment as above), it will be replaced by the text `Some text`. For example:
```
cmdline: something before ${MY_MACRO} something after
```

Macros must always be placed inside `${...}` where `...` is the arbitrary macro
name.

### Built-in macros

Limine automatically defines these macros:

* `ARCH` - This built-in macro expands to the architecture of the machine.
  Possible values are: `x86-64`, `ia-32`, `aarch64`, `riscv64`, `loongarch64`.
  In the case of IA-32, BIOS or UEFI, the macro will always expand to `x86-64`
  if the 64-bit extensions are available, else `ia-32`.
* `FW_TYPE` - This built-in macro expands to `UEFI` if booted using UEFI
  firmware, or `BIOS` if booted using legacy x86 BIOS.
* `LOADER_ARCH` - This built-in macro expands to the architecture of the Limine
  binary itself. Possible values are the same as `ARCH`: `x86-64`, `ia-32`,
  `aarch64`, `riscv64`, `loongarch64`. Unlike `ARCH`, this is determined at
  compile time and does not probe CPU capabilities; the IA-32 binary always
  expands to `ia-32` even on a CPU with 64-bit extensions.

### # Crabshell and the early RAM filesystem › ## Tests and limitations › L71-72
```
Host-side tests cover path traversal, file create/write/append/copy/move/remove, entry kinds, path rendering, directory emptiness, and the parser's syntax/arity. The QEMU smoke test checks that the serial shell reaches its prompt; it does not emulate reboot persistence or prove isolation. ```

### # Building Rustix › ## Building and smoke-testing a boot image › L43-44

`just smoke` launches `target/rustix.iso` in `qemu-system-x86_64` with a 256 MiB q35 machine, headless display, captured COM1 output, and a 20-second deadline. QEMU is expected to remain running at the interactive shell; the runner terminates it at the deadline and requires the startup banner, Crabshell-ready message, and initial prompt. On a failure it prints the serial log. The log remains at `target/rustix-qemu-serial.log` for inspection.

```

### # Rustix documentation › ## Current status › L20-21
```
The repository contains a bare-metal `no_std` Rust kernel for `x86_64-unknown-none`. After Limine handoff it validates and copies memory-map metadata into an owned snapshot, reports baseline CPUID features, seeds a volatile RAM filesystem, and runs Crabshell over the COM1 serial console. Crabshell's allocation-free parser is a separate crate; the kernel handles command execution. The image builder and bounded QEMU prompt smoke test are wired into CI, but the latest source changes have not yet been built or boot-tested and Milestone 0's end-to-end run remains pending. This is a kernel-mode shell, not a user process. A bounded physical-frame allocator core is initialized from the validated map and reported by `meminfo`, but no kernel service allocates or maps frames yet; there is not yet page-table management, a heap, a general IRQ subsystem, a scheduler, process isolation, a persistent filesystem, or a Unix compatibility layer. Fatal CPU exceptions have basic GDT/TSS/IDT diagnostics but no recovery or fault-injection tests yet.

```

```rustix/docs/architecture/boot.md
    28	See [`../development/building.md`](../development/building.md) for commands and toolchain setup.
    29	
    30	## Failure behavior and limitations
    31	
    32	Missing responses, bad pointers/alignment, invalid HHDM values, excessive counts, null entries, address arithmetic overflow, and invalid or overlapping physical ranges reject the complete boot snapshot. `_start` halts before starting Crabshell rather than continuing with partial memory metadata. Structural checks cannot establish that a non-null loader pointer is mapped and readable; that remains an explicit trust assumption of the Limine handoff. The installed exception handlers print fatal context and halt; no fault recovery or maskable IRQ delivery is provided. COM1 writes use a bounded polling loop so a non-responsive UART does not block forever.
    33	
    34	The repository now includes a Limine v12.9.3 binary archive pin with SHA-256 verification, a hybrid ISO recipe, and a bounded QEMU serial smoke test that checks Crabshell's prompt. These workflows are automated in CI, but the boot milestone is not considered complete until that end-to-end job passes. There is still no framebuffer console, reboot/shutdown interface, or broader boot-protocol compatibility test. The available serial and keyboard drivers do not imply a general device model.
    35	
    36	## Future boot work
    37	
    38	The kernel now snapshots and validates the Limine map and preserves firmware and loader-reclaimable classifications without reclaiming them. No region is considered Rustix-owned or free for allocation yet. Loader-reclaimable memory must remain unavailable until Rustix has copied any needed boot data and explicitly reaches a documented reclaim point; ACPI reclaimable memory needs the ACPI tables to be copied or parsed first. Frame allocation, page-table replacement, and ownership transfer remain future work.

```

     3	These instructions apply to every coding agent working in this repository. Read this file before changing code. For the architecture and detailed subsystem contracts, use the linked documents under `docs/`; this file summarizes the rules agents must preserve.

     6	
     7	Rustix is an experimental 64-bit, Unix-like operating system with its own Rust kernel. Limine is the external boot protocol/loader only. Do not describe Limine, a host shell, or a userspace project as the Rustix kernel.
     8	
     9	The kernel is `no_std` and targets `x86_64-unknown-none`. Rust is the implementation language for kernel and OS components. The repository currently uses a Python standard-library script only to assemble and smoke-test the boot image; it does not replace kernel or OS functionality.
    10	
    11	Unix-like behavior is a long-term design goal, not a claim of POSIX compatibility. Make unsupported behavior explicit rather than approximating it silently.

    22	- Bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT setup and fatal exception handlers for vectors 0–31. Double faults use an IST stack and page faults report CR2. Maskable IRQs remain disabled; exception recovery and fault-injection tests are not implemented.

    29	- There is no scheduler, userspace, syscall ABI, persistent filesystem, user/kernel isolation, or general IRQ subsystem.

    50

    52	- `src/boot.rs` — mutable Limine requests, structural response/range validation, owned `BootInfo`, and boot diagnostics.
    53	- `src/memory.rs` — allocation-free memory-map validation and known/unknown region classification.
    54	- `src/frame.rs` — bounded physical-frame allocator core; it only uses validated `Usable` ranges, reserves the first MiB, and has fixed range metadata.
    55	- `src/shell.rs` — serial line editor and kernel-side Crabshell executor.
    56	- `src/vfs.rs` — fixed-capacity volatile RAM filesystem and host-side tests.
    57	- `crates/crabshell/` — separate `no_std` parser crate. It has no terminal, filesystem, or kernel dependencies.
    58	- `src/arch/x86_64/serial.rs` — polling COM1 driver for shell input/output.
    59	- `src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs` — bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT, assembly stubs, and fatal exception diagnostics.
    60	- `src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs` — CPUID identification and selected feature reporting.
    61	- `src/arch/x86_64/keyboard.rs` — raw, non-blocking PS/2-compatible scancode polling; not an input subsystem.
    62	- `src/arch/x86_64/io.rs` — narrow port-I/O wrappers.

    65	- `justfile` — supported development commands.
    66	- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — CI validation workflow.
    67	
    68	## Engineering rules
    69	
    70	### Keep changes incremental and coherent
    71	
    72	1. Inspect the relevant source, tests, docs, and call sites before editing.
    73	2. State assumptions, invariants, and failure behavior for new kernel interfaces.
    74	3. Prefer small vertical slices that compile and can be tested over broad scaffolding or placeholder APIs.
    75	4. Update tests and documentation alongside behavior changes.
    76	5. Do not change unrelated code, rename files gratuitously, add speculative features, or rewrite project history.
    77	6. Do not commit or create branches unless the user explicitly asks.
    78	
    79	### Rust and dependency policy
    80	
    81	- Preserve the kernel's `no_std`/freestanding constraints. Do not introduce `std` into kernel code.
    82	- Prefer `core` and existing in-tree abstractions. Do not add third-party Rust dependencies without a concrete need and compatibility/security review.
    83	- Keep the Crabshell parser independent of kernel I/O and VFS implementation. Kernel execution belongs in `src/shell.rs` or an appropriate kernel service.
    84	- Do not add allocation-dependent APIs before a real heap exists. Fixed-capacity structures must document their limits and exhaustion behavior.
    85	- Respect the workspace structure and the host-testable `rustix-kernel` library versus freestanding `rustix` binary boundary.
    86	
    87	### Unsafe and hardware code
    88	
    89	Unsafe code is expected only at explicit hardware, boot-protocol, assembly, or raw-memory boundaries. Keep each unsafe block narrow and document the invariant that makes it sound. Do not add broad `unsafe impl`, mutable global references, unchecked pointer arithmetic, or unreviewed inline/global assembly.
    90	
    91	Before changing boot or memory code, account for these facts:
    92	
    93	- Limine fills response pointers before `_start`; the request records must remain writable in the ELF image.
    94	- Rustix validates nullness, alignment, counts, arithmetic, and physical ranges, but cannot prove that a non-null bootloader pointer is readable.
    95	- Physical ranges are half-open `[start, end)` and must use checked arithmetic.
    96	- Only regions classified `Usable` may enter the frame allocator. ACPI, bootloader-reclaimable, framebuffer, reserved, unknown, and other types are not free frames.
    97	- A `Frame` is a physical address, not a dereferenceable pointer. Do not access it through the HHDM or change CR3 until an explicit, reviewed mapping policy and ownership proof exist.
    98	- The kernel currently inherits Limine's page tables. Do not casually replace or mutate them: preserve the executing kernel, boot stack, `BootInfo`, request/response data, exception stacks, and mappings needed to continue execution.
    99	- The exception setup is fatal-only. It does not enable maskable interrupts, configure a PIC/APIC, or provide recovery. Do not call `sti` or claim interrupt support without an IRQ design and tests.
   100	- The shell and VFS run in ring 0 and are not isolated or secure.
   101	
   102	For hardware changes, document assumptions about CPU mode, selectors, stacks, page permissions, interrupt state, and failure handling. Avoid new architecture mechanisms that cannot be statically reviewed or validated.
   103	
   104	### Shell and filesystem contract
   105	
   106	- Crabshell is presently a kernel-mode serial shell, not a userspace program or a POSIX shell.
   107	- Its parser is a separate `no_std`, allocation-free crate; retain that boundary.
   108	- The RAM filesystem is volatile and bounded. Preserve explicit errors and test capacity, path, and mutation edge cases.
   109	- Do not imply persistence, permissions, links, process launching, or shell features that do not exist.
   110	- Update the parser tests and `docs/architecture/crabshell.md` when adding or changing commands.
   111	
   112	## Validation workflow
   113	
   114	Run the narrowest relevant checks first, then broaden them. From the repository root, the supported commands are:
   115	
   116	```sh
   117	just fmt
   118	just test
   119	just check
   120	just build
   121	just image
   122	just smoke
   123	just verify
   124	```
   125	
   126	`just test` runs host-side library tests (memory-map validation, frame allocator, VFS, and Crabshell parser). `just check` checks `x86_64-unknown-none`; `just build` links the optimized ELF. `just verify` includes formatting, host tests, target check, pinned Limine image creation, and QEMU prompt smoke test. Image/boot checks need Python, `xorriso`, QEMU, the Rust target, and network access for the first pinned Limine download.
   127	
   128	For changes to `src/main.rs`, `src/boot.rs`, linker/request configuration, `src/arch/x86_64/`, `src/frame.rs`, or paging/heap code, the intended full validation is `just verify`. If the environment does not permit a check, report the exact blocker and leave the corresponding roadmap criterion pending.
   129	
   130	Do not claim a check passed unless it was run and its successful result was observed. Editor diagnostics are useful but are not a substitute for `cargo test`, a target build, or QEMU. A target check is not a final link; a linked ELF is not proof of boot; a prompt smoke test is not proof of interactive shell behavior or physical-hardware correctness.
   131	
   132	## Completion criteria for agent changes
   133	
   134	Before reporting work complete:
   135	
   136	- Ensure source, tests, docs, and call sites agree.
   137	- Review unsafe and hardware assumptions, including error paths and capacity limits.
   138	- Run appropriate formatting/tests/build/boot checks, or clearly state why they could not run.
   139	- Report files changed, behavior delivered, validation actually observed, and remaining risks.
   140	- Keep milestone status accurate. A subsystem is not complete just because it has code.

# Rustix agent instructions

These instructions apply to every coding agent working in this repository. Read this file before changing code. For the architecture and detailed subsystem contracts, use the linked documents under `docs/`; this file summarizes the rules agents must preserve.

## Project mission

Rustix is an experimental 64-bit, Unix-like operating system with its own Rust kernel. Limine is the external boot protocol/loader only. Do not describe Limine, a host shell, or a userspace project as the Rustix kernel.

The kernel is `no_std` and targets `x86_64-unknown-none`. Rust is the implementation language for kernel and OS components. The repository currently uses a Python standard-library script only to assemble and smoke-test the boot image; it does not replace kernel or OS functionality.

Unix-like behavior is a long-term design goal, not a claim of POSIX compatibility. Make unsupported behavior explicit rather than approximating it silently.

## Current project status — read before planning

The source contains:

- A Limine-based x86_64 kernel entry, linker layout, serial diagnostics, and boot-memory reporting.
- A separate allocation-free `no_std` `crabshell` parser crate and a kernel-mode COM1 shell frontend.
- A volatile, fixed-capacity RAM filesystem used by the shell.
- A validated, fixed-capacity boot memory-map snapshot and baseline CPUID reporting.
- A fixed-capacity physical frame allocator retained in `BootInfo`; Crabshell's `meminfo` command reports counts. No kernel service currently allocates frames for mappings or other services.
- Bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT setup and fatal exception handlers for vectors 0–31. Double faults use an IST stack and page faults report CR2. Maskable IRQs remain disabled; exception recovery and fault-injection tests are not implemented.

Important incomplete work:

- `just verify` passed for the current working tree in WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 on 2026-10-16: formatting, 19 host tests, target check, optimized build, image creation, and the 20-second QEMU prompt smoke test. A clean-checkout run with an uncached build/tool state and a CI run remain outstanding.
- The boot snapshot tests and QEMU boot-metadata reporting path have now been exercised. Structural pointer checks still cannot prove that a Limine-provided non-null pointer is mapped or readable; that remains a loader trust boundary.
- Milestone 2 is **in progress**, not complete. Rustix still inherits Limine's page tables; it has no kernel-owned page-table manager, no heap, and no live frame-allocation callers. The descriptor setup reaches the shell in QEMU, but exception handlers have not had fault-injection testing.
- There is no scheduler, userspace, syscall ABI, persistent filesystem, user/kernel isolation, or general IRQ subsystem.

Never advance status or check off a roadmap item merely because source code or an interface exists. Update `docs/roadmap/README.md` only to reflect implementation and validation actually achieved.

## Source-of-truth documents

Consult the relevant documentation before modifying a subsystem:

- [`docs/index.md`](docs/index.md) — documentation entry point and current status.
- [`docs/roadmap/README.md`](docs/roadmap/README.md) — milestone sequencing and exit criteria.
- [`docs/architecture/overview.md`](docs/architecture/overview.md) — current architecture and intended layers.
- [`docs/architecture/boot.md`](docs/architecture/boot.md) — Limine requests, boot snapshot, and trust boundary.
- [`docs/architecture/memory.md`](docs/architecture/memory.md) — memory ownership, frame allocator, and paging direction.
- [`docs/architecture/crabshell.md`](docs/architecture/crabshell.md) — parser/kernel boundary and shell/VFS contract.
- [`docs/architecture/drivers.md`](docs/architecture/drivers.md) — current driver scope and limitations.
- [`docs/security.md`](docs/security.md) — unsafe boundaries and security policy.
- [`docs/development/building.md`](docs/development/building.md) and [`docs/development/testing.md`](docs/development/testing.md) — supported commands and validation expectations.

When code and documentation disagree, inspect the implementation, resolve the discrepancy deliberately, and update the relevant documentation in the same change.

## Repository map

- `src/main.rs` — freestanding entry, boot snapshot acquisition, panic path, and shell handoff.
- `src/boot.rs` — mutable Limine requests, structural response/range validation, owned `BootInfo`, and boot diagnostics.
- `src/memory.rs` — allocation-free memory-map validation and known/unknown region classification.
- `src/frame.rs` — bounded physical-frame allocator core; it only uses validated `Usable` ranges, reserves the first MiB, and has fixed range metadata.
- `src/shell.rs` — serial line editor and kernel-side Crabshell executor.
- `src/vfs.rs` — fixed-capacity volatile RAM filesystem and host-side tests.
- `crates/crabshell/` — separate `no_std` parser crate. It has no terminal, filesystem, or kernel dependencies.
- `src/arch/x86_64/serial.rs` — polling COM1 driver for shell input/output.
- `src/arch/x86_64/interrupts.rs` — bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT, assembly stubs, and fatal exception diagnostics.
- `src/arch/x86_64/cpu.rs` — CPUID identification and selected feature reporting.
- `src/arch/x86_64/keyboard.rs` — raw, non-blocking PS/2-compatible scancode polling; not an input subsystem.
- `src/arch/x86_64/io.rs` — narrow port-I/O wrappers.
- `linker.ld`, `.cargo/config.toml`, `rust-toolchain.toml` — target, linker, and toolchain configuration.
- `limine.conf`, `scripts/boot.py` — boot configuration and pinned image/emulator workflow.
- `justfile` — supported development commands.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — CI validation workflow.

## Engineering rules

### Keep changes incremental and coherent

1. Inspect the relevant source, tests, docs, and call sites before editing.
2. State assumptions, invariants, and failure behavior for new kernel interfaces.
3. Prefer small vertical slices that compile and can be tested over broad scaffolding or placeholder APIs.
4. Update tests and documentation alongside behavior changes.
5. Do not change unrelated code, rename files gratuitously, add speculative features, or rewrite project history.
6. Do not commit or create branches unless the user explicitly asks.

### Rust and dependency policy

- Preserve the kernel's `no_std`/freestanding constraints. Do not introduce `std` into kernel code.
- Prefer `core` and existing in-tree abstractions. Do not add third-party Rust dependencies without a concrete need and compatibility/security review.
- Keep the Crabshell parser independent of kernel I/O and VFS implementation. Kernel execution belongs in `src/shell.rs` or an appropriate kernel service.
- Do not add allocation-dependent APIs before a real heap exists. Fixed-capacity structures must document their limits and exhaustion behavior.
- Respect the workspace structure and the host-testable `rustix-kernel` library versus freestanding `rustix` binary boundary.

### Unsafe and hardware code

Unsafe code is expected only at explicit hardware, boot-protocol, assembly, or raw-memory boundaries. Keep each unsafe block narrow and document the invariant that makes it sound. Do not add broad `unsafe impl`, mutable global references, unchecked pointer arithmetic, or unreviewed inline/global assembly.

Before changing boot or memory code, account for these facts:

- Limine fills response pointers before `_start`; the request records must remain writable in the ELF image.
- Rustix validates nullness, alignment, counts, arithmetic, and physical ranges, but cannot prove that a non-null bootloader pointer is readable.
- Physical ranges are half-open `[start, end)` and must use checked arithmetic.
- Only regions classified `Usable` may enter the frame allocator. ACPI, bootloader-reclaimable, framebuffer, reserved, unknown, and other types are not free frames.
- A `Frame` is a physical address, not a dereferenceable pointer. Do not access it through the HHDM or change CR3 until an explicit, reviewed mapping policy and ownership proof exist.
- The kernel currently inherits Limine's page tables. Do not casually replace or mutate them: preserve the executing kernel, boot stack, `BootInfo`, request/response data, exception stacks, and mappings needed to continue execution.
- The exception setup is fatal-only. It does not enable maskable interrupts, configure a PIC/APIC, or provide recovery. Do not call `sti` or claim interrupt support without an IRQ design and tests.
- The shell and VFS run in ring 0 and are not isolated or secure.

For hardware changes, document assumptions about CPU mode, selectors, stacks, page permissions, interrupt state, and failure handling. Avoid new architecture mechanisms that cannot be statically reviewed or validated.

### Shell and filesystem contract

- Crabshell is presently a kernel-mode serial shell, not a userspace program or a POSIX shell.
- Its parser is a separate `no_std`, allocation-free crate; retain that boundary.
- The RAM filesystem is volatile and bounded. Preserve explicit errors and test capacity, path, and mutation edge cases.
- Do not imply persistence, permissions, links, process launching, or shell features that do not exist.
- Update the parser tests and `docs/architecture/crabshell.md` when adding or changing commands.

## Validation workflow

Run the narrowest relevant checks first, then broaden them. From the repository root, the supported commands are:

```sh
just fmt
just test
just check
just build
just image
just smoke
just verify
```

`just test` runs host-side library tests (memory-map validation, frame allocator, VFS, and Crabshell parser). `just check` checks `x86_64-unknown-none`; `just build` links the optimized ELF. `just verify` includes formatting, host tests, target check, pinned Limine image creation, and QEMU prompt smoke test. Image/boot checks need Python, `xorriso`, QEMU, the Rust target, and network access for the first pinned Limine download.

For changes to `src/main.rs`, `src/boot.rs`, linker/request configuration, `src/arch/x86_64/`, `src/frame.rs`, or paging/heap code, the intended full validation is `just verify`. If the environment does not permit a check, report the exact blocker and leave the corresponding roadmap criterion pending.

Do not claim a check passed unless it was run and its successful result was observed. Editor diagnostics are useful but are not a substitute for `cargo test`, a target build, or QEMU. A target check is not a final link; a linked ELF is not proof of boot; a prompt smoke test is not proof of interactive shell behavior or physical-hardware correctness.

## Completion criteria for agent changes

Before reporting work complete:

- Ensure source, tests, docs, and call sites agree.
- Review unsafe and hardware assumptions, including error paths and capacity limits.
- Run appropriate formatting/tests/build/boot checks, or clearly state why they could not run.
- Report files changed, behavior delivered, validation actually observed, and remaining risks.
- Keep milestone status accurate. A subsystem is not complete just because it has code.

# Rustix documentation

Rustix is a 64-bit, Rust-first, Unix-like operating-system project. This index separates current implementation facts from planned interfaces: roadmap items are proposals until the corresponding code and tests exist.

## Start here

- [Project and implementation overview](architecture/overview.md)
- [Boot protocol and current entry path](architecture/boot.md)
- [Memory-management direction](architecture/memory.md)
- [x86_64 drivers and hardware boundary](architecture/drivers.md)
- [Crabshell and the volatile RAM filesystem](architecture/crabshell.md)
- [Unix-like process and syscall direction](architecture/syscall-abi.md)
- [Build and toolchain guide](development/building.md)
- [Testing and verification](development/testing.md)
- [Security and unsafe-code policy](security.md)
- [Milestones and acceptance criteria](roadmap/README.md)

## Current status

The repository contains a bare-metal `no_std` Rust kernel for `x86_64-unknown-none`. After Limine handoff it validates and copies memory-map metadata into an owned snapshot, reports baseline CPUID features, seeds a volatile RAM filesystem, and runs Crabshell over the COM1 serial console. Crabshell's allocation-free parser is a separate crate; the kernel handles command execution. On 2026-10-16, `just verify` passed in WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 for the current working tree, including image creation and a bounded QEMU boot to the shell prompt; the serial log showed memory-map and CPU reporting. A clean-checkout run with uncached build/tool state and a CI run remain pending. This is a kernel-mode shell, not a user process. A bounded physical-frame allocator core is initialized from the validated map and reported by `meminfo`, but no kernel service allocates or maps frames yet; there is not yet page-table management, a heap, a general IRQ subsystem, a scheduler, process isolation, a persistent filesystem, or a Unix compatibility layer. Fatal CPU exceptions have basic GDT/TSS/IDT diagnostics but no recovery or fault-injection tests yet.

## Documentation conventions

- **Implemented** means present in the repository and checked by current code or tests.
- **Planned** means an architectural direction, not a stable ABI or delivered capability.
- Any future ABI proposal must state versioning, error behavior, memory ownership, and compatibility expectations before it is treated as stable.

# Rustix roadmap

This roadmap describes an incremental path from the current bare-metal kernel to a useful Unix-like operating system. It is a dependency plan, not a schedule or a claim of compatibility. Features become current only after the implementation, tests, and exit criteria below agree.

## How to read status

- A checked box means the source/design work exists; it does **not** imply the code compiled, linked, booted, or passed an integration test.
- A milestone is not complete until its stated exit criteria are met and the evidence is recorded.
- Hardware work needs target build and emulator evidence. Host tests cannot validate privileged instructions, bootloader pointers, page tables, device I/O, or exception-entry assembly.
- Future work is intentionally not represented by placeholder APIs or dummy implementations.

## Current status

- **Milestone 0: current working tree passes `just verify`; clean-checkout reproducibility remains pending.** The WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 run on 2026-10-16 built the image and reached the Crabshell prompt in QEMU. A fresh checkout with uncached build/tool state and a CI run have not yet been tested.
- **Milestone 1: host validation and QEMU boot-metadata reporting have been exercised.** The bounded boot snapshot, memory-range classification, and CPUID reporting were covered by `just verify`; the Limine pointer-readability trust boundary remains explicit.
- **Milestone 2: in progress, not complete.** A bounded frame allocator is retained in `BootInfo`, and bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT fatal exception handlers exist. The kernel still inherits Limine's page tables; there is no owned page-table manager, global heap, live frame-allocation caller, or fault-injection/emulator validation.
- **Milestones 3 and later: planned.** There is no general IRQ system, scheduler, userspace, syscall ABI, persistent filesystem, GUI, or networking stack.

## Dependency path

```text
Reliable boot
    -> validated boot state
    -> owned mappings + frame allocation + heap + fault diagnostics
    -> timer/IRQ model + scheduler
    -> isolated processes + syscall ABI
    -> VFS/storage + userland utilities
    -> graphical terminal and other optional services
```

Some device-driver work can proceed in parallel after the core ownership, locking, and testing rules exist. It must not bypass them with direct, unreviewed hardware access.

---

## Milestone 0 — repeatable Rust kernel boot (current baseline)

### Implementation present

- [x] `no_std` Rust kernel binary for `x86_64-unknown-none` with its own ELF linker layout and `_start`.
- [x] Limine boot requests and documented external-loader boundary.
- [x] COM1 serial output/input, startup reporting, and panic/fatal halt path.
- [x] Narrow x86 port-I/O helpers and raw non-blocking PS/2-compatible scancode polling.
- [x] `just` tasks for formatting, host tests, target checks, ELF/image builds, and QEMU smoke/run workflows.
- [x] Pinned Limine v12.9.3 binary archive with SHA-256 verification, BIOS/UEFI hybrid image recipe, and CI workflow.
- [x] Separate allocation-free Crabshell parser, kernel serial frontend, and bounded volatile RAM filesystem.

### Validation evidence and remaining proof

- [x] Current source passed formatting, host tests, target check, and optimized build through `just verify`.
- [x] The pinned image built and the bounded QEMU smoke test reached the Crabshell prompt in WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 on 2026-10-16.
- [ ] Repeat verification from a clean checkout with uncached build/tool state; CI has not yet been observed.

The QEMU serial log showed the startup banner, HHDM offset, validated memory-map summary, frame counts, CPUID report, and initial prompt. If a future smoke test fails, preserve `target/rustix-qemu-serial.log` as failure evidence.

**Exit criteria:** a clean checkout builds the image, reaches `_start`, reports the expected startup state, and reaches the Crabshell prompt in the automated QEMU test. The current working tree meets the boot path checks; clean-checkout reproducibility is still pending.

---

## Milestone 1 — validated boot state and machine diagnostics (validation exercised)

### Source work present

- [x] Copy Limine HHDM and memory-map information into an owned `BootInfo` before shell startup.
- [x] Bound map entries; check pointer nullness/alignment, count conversion, arithmetic, nonzero ranges, and overlap.
- [x] Convert ranges to half-open `[start, end)` physical intervals.
- [x] Preserve usable, reserved, ACPI, bad-memory, bootloader-reclaimable, executable/module, framebuffer, and unknown region classifications.

- [x] Report baseline CPUID vendor/features and document the current COM1-only console.
- [x] Document that classifying a range does not transfer ownership or authorize access/reclamation.

### Remaining proof and polish

- [x] Host tests cover malformed and boundary memory-map values, including empty input, capacity, zero length, overflow, overlap, adjacency, and unknown types.
- [ ] Add serial/report formatting tests if output formatting is separated into a host-testable pure helper.
- [x] Build and boot the image with the current request-section/linker layout; the QEMU serial log showed the boot metadata and CPUID report.
- [ ] Revisit loader pointer validation before introducing another boot source: numeric checks cannot prove non-null response data is mapped and readable.

**Exit criteria:** the host tests and QEMU metadata/reporting path were observed in the 2026-10-16 WSL2 `just verify` run. The loader readability trust boundary remains documented; clean-checkout reproducibility is tracked under Milestone 0.

## Milestone 2 — memory ownership, paging, heap, and exceptions (in progress)

This milestone must establish a safe basis for future allocation and kernel services. Do not allocate a frame for a mapping or dereference it through the HHDM until the mapping/ownership proof is explicit.

### Source work present

- [x] Fixed-capacity frame allocator over validated `Usable` ranges, with page alignment, first-MiB reservation, deallocation, coalescing, bounded metadata, and host tests (`src/frame.rs`).
- [x] Initialize allocator metadata from the boot snapshot and expose counts through Crabshell `meminfo`.
- [x] Bootstrap GDT/TSS/IDT and fatal handlers for exception vectors 0–31.
- [x] Give double faults a dedicated IST stack; report saved register/error context and CR2/error bits for page faults.
- [x] Keep maskable IRQ delivery disabled; current exception handling is fatal-only.

### Required memory-management work

- [ ] Specify how one allocator instance owns its ranges, how allocated frames are returned, and how exhaustion/metadata exhaustion is surfaced to callers.
- [ ] Document the active virtual-address width, HHDM coverage, physical-address width, page size, and the policy for MMIO, guard regions, kernel image, stacks, boot data, and page-table frames.
- [ ] Design a kernel-owned page-table transition that preserves every mapping needed to execute during and after the switch: kernel text/data/BSS, current stack, `BootInfo`, Limine requests/responses still needed, GDT/TSS/IDT, exception stacks, serial state, and any direct-map access used by the transition.
- [ ] Implement checked page-table entry construction and mapping operations: canonical/aligned addresses, permissions, cache attributes, ownership, huge-page behavior, and explicit writable-executable rejection by default.
- [ ] Ensure mapping failure (including no free frame or range-table exhaustion) rolls back partial page-table allocations or leaves the old map active.
- [ ] Add host tests for mapping/address policy and allocator failure invariants. Add a reviewable emulator test for mapping, unmapping, permission behavior, and frame reclamation before replacing the inherited CR3.
- [ ] Only after a mapping policy works, add a kernel heap with documented alignment, allocation/free semantics, deterministic exhaustion behavior, and an explicit rule for interrupt contexts.

### Required exception/descriptor validation

- [x] Source contains GDT/TSS/IDT setup and normalized stubs for architectural exception vectors 0–31; double fault uses IST1.
- [ ] Target-assemble and link the stubs; inspect descriptor layout/selectors and verify call-stack alignment and error-code normalization.
- [ ] Add fault-injection tests for at least a controlled page fault and a controlled exception. Confirm diagnostics are captured and the kernel halts rather than returning.
- [ ] Confirm the descriptor setup and exception paths boot in QEMU before relying on them as a memory-management safety net.

**Exit criteria:** the kernel owns and validates its page-table state, frame allocation/mapping invariants are tested, OOM/failure leaves memory state consistent, page faults are diagnosable, and the kernel remains bootable under emulator tests. Not met: page tables, heap, fault-injection, and boot verification remain outstanding.

---

## Milestone 3 — IRQs, time, and kernel scheduling

Do not enable interrupts as a side effect of installing exception gates. IRQ delivery needs its own controller, acknowledgement, masking, ownership, and synchronization design.

### Planned work

- [ ] Select and document the initial interrupt controller policy for QEMU and target hardware (for example, legacy PIC compatibility versus local I/O APIC; do not enable both accidentally).
- [ ] Add IRQ vector allocation, controller masking/unmasking, end-of-interrupt acknowledgement, spurious-interrupt handling, and a policy for unexpected IRQs.
- [ ] Add a calibrated/verified timer source and monotonic timekeeping; test interval arithmetic and drift assumptions.
- [ ] Establish interrupt-safe lock primitives and rules for code callable from normal, exception, and IRQ contexts. No allocator or blocking console operation may run in an unsafe interrupt context.
- [ ] Add a minimal kernel-thread context and lifecycle model, stack ownership/guard policy, context-switch tests, and emulator scheduling tests.
- [ ] Add preemption only after lock, stack, timer, and interrupt-return invariants have deterministic tests.
- [ ] Keep application-processor startup/SMP as a separate sub-milestone after per-CPU state, TLB invalidation, and lock semantics exist.

**Exit criteria:** tested IRQ acknowledgement and timer behavior, deterministic thread lifecycle/context-switch tests, and bounded QEMU tests under repeated timer interrupts. No `sti` before the design and tests are ready.

---

## Milestone 4 — isolated processes and syscall ABI

Userspace begins only after page tables, exception handling, scheduling, and controlled memory allocation are trustworthy. The syscall ABI is a product interface and must not emerge accidentally from internal functions.

### Planned work

- [ ] Decide and document the x86_64 user-entry/syscall mechanism, register convention, selector/MSR setup, per-CPU state requirements, and safe return path.
- [ ] Add user/kernel page permissions and process-owned address spaces, including teardown and TLB invalidation rules.
- [ ] Implement copy-in/copy-out helpers that validate lengths, arithmetic, canonical ranges, permissions, and faults; never form a kernel reference directly from a user pointer.
- [ ] Specify version discovery, stable syscall numbers, argument layouts, error encoding, partial-I/O behavior, interruption/restart, and compatibility policy before exposing calls.
- [ ] Add initial process lifecycle and descriptor-table semantics: create/load, exit, wait, close, duplication/inheritance, and process cleanup.
- [ ] Load a deliberately small documented executable format with bounds/segment/permission checks; reject malformed binaries safely.
- [ ] Build adversarial tests for bad pointers, overflow, invalid mappings, process teardown, descriptor misuse, and failed exec.

### First user-visible target

A small controlled `init` process should start from a reproducible image, write through a descriptor, exit with a status, and be waited on by a kernel test harness. Do not claim userspace or process isolation from ring-0 tasks that merely use process-shaped structs.

**Exit criteria:** an isolated init process runs in user mode and uses a versioned, documented syscall subset; invalid user pointers and process teardown are tested without corrupting the kernel.

---

## Milestone 5 — VFS, storage, and device ownership

Keep the current RAM filesystem as a bootstrap/test implementation. Persistence and device drivers require explicit block ownership, error handling, and recovery behavior.

### Planned work

- [ ] Define VFS node, mount, path, metadata, and file-descriptor contracts independently of a particular disk format.
- [ ] Preserve volatile RAMFS as a test backend and add tests for mount/path errors, capacity, partial I/O, and object lifetime.
- [ ] Add a narrowly scoped block-device interface with request validation, timeout/error reporting, and a QEMU-supported initial device driver (such as virtio-blk after PCI discovery is ready).
- [ ] Choose and document the first on-disk filesystem format. Specify partition discovery, byte order, block size, metadata limits, corruption handling, and read-only/recovery behavior before writable support.
- [ ] Add persistent write/read/remount/reboot integration tests; never claim persistence from an in-memory cache alone.
- [ ] Add a driver ownership and DMA policy before any device can write into arbitrary kernel memory.
- [ ] Define file descriptors and basic process I/O semantics before exposing them to applications.

**Exit criteria:** a reproducible image mounts a documented on-disk filesystem, user-visible tools can create/read files across reboot, and corruption/I/O errors fail safely.

---

## Milestone 6 — initial userspace and command-line utilities

Crabshell is currently an in-kernel parser/frontend. The long-term terminal application should reuse its parser model without linking kernel internals or bypassing syscalls.

### Planned work

- [ ] Start a user-mode `init` process and establish executable search, environment, current directory, descriptor inheritance, and process startup rules.
- [ ] Port or adapt Crabshell into a userspace terminal application that uses only the documented syscall/VFS interfaces.
- [ ] Add a small utility set with explicit scope: file listing, text output, create/remove/copy/move, and system information.
- [ ] Add command-line quoting, escaping, history, redirection, and pipelines only with parser tests and process/descriptor/pipe semantics to support them.
- [ ] Add integration tests that launch tools from the filesystem image and exercise them through syscalls; keep unsupported features explicit.

**Exit criteria:** shell and basic tools run as isolated user processes from a reproducible image; no shell command directly calls kernel-private VFS internals.

---

## Milestone 7 — graphical console and GUI (long-term)

A GUI is intentionally downstream of stable memory management, interrupts/input, process isolation, drivers, and userspace. Keep Crabshell's parser independent so a graphical terminal frontend can reuse it.

### Planned work

- [ ] Add validated framebuffer discovery and memory ownership; implement a minimal text/graphics console without compromising serial panic diagnostics.
- [ ] Establish an input subsystem that separates raw device events from key mapping and terminal policy. Plan PS/2 and USB HID support separately; do not treat the current raw scancode poller as a keyboard driver stack.
- [ ] Define a graphics buffer ownership/presentation API, clipping rules, pixel format, and bounds/overflow checks.
- [ ] Implement a minimal compositor/windowing policy only after process isolation and input routing are ready.
- [ ] Run Crabshell as a terminal application in a GUI window using the same parser and userspace services as the serial/TTY path.
- [ ] Preserve serial as a headless recovery/debug console and add repeatable QEMU display/input tests.

**Exit criteria:** a documented GUI session starts from userspace, renders a terminal, accepts tested input, and does not require direct kernel-private VFS access.

---

## Milestone 8 — networking (long-term, after drivers and process isolation)

Networking is not implied by the current device drivers. The initial target should be a tightly scoped virtual-device path with clear ownership and bounded buffers.

### Planned work

- [ ] Complete PCI/device discovery and define DMA buffer ownership, address translation, cache synchronization, and reset/error behavior.
- [ ] Implement one virtual NIC driver with bounded queues and timeouts; test against QEMU user networking.
- [ ] Choose and document a minimal link/network protocol scope before implementation. Keep packet parsing length-checked and fuzzable on the host.
- [ ] Add interface configuration, routing, socket/descriptor ownership, and per-process access policy.
- [ ] Add adversarial packet tests and integration tests for link loss, malformed packets, queue exhaustion, and device reset.
- [ ] Add higher-level transports/services only when the required protocol semantics, entropy source, and security model are designed.

**Exit criteria:** documented user processes can communicate through a tested virtual NIC/network stack, with malformed input and resource exhaustion handled safely. Do not claim internet, TLS, or POSIX sockets merely from a packet driver.

---

## Cross-cutting acceptance gates

Every milestone should include the relevant subset of these gates:

1. **Design:** documented ownership, invariants, resource limits, error semantics, and unsupported cases.
2. **Tests:** host tests for pure policy and malformed/boundary input; integration tests for hardware-facing behavior.
3. **Safety:** review unsafe blocks, pointer provenance/access, integer overflow, privilege boundaries, concurrency, and cleanup/rollback paths.
4. **Build:** format, host tests, target check, and final ELF link as appropriate.
5. **Boot/integration:** QEMU tests for changes to boot, paging, descriptors, interrupts, drivers, processes, or persistence.
6. **Documentation/status:** update architecture and roadmap docs; never check off a criterion without evidence.
7. **Compatibility:** claim Unix/POSIX behavior only for the exact documented subset with conformance-style tests.

## Working rule

Prefer a small end-to-end vertical slice over broad, unbootable scaffolding. A source file, interface, or architecture document is not proof that the corresponding subsystem is operational. When a check cannot run, record the exact environment blocker and leave that acceptance gate pending.

# Boot protocol and kernel entry

## Current boot contract

Rustix currently expects a Limine-compatible x86_64 handoff. Limine is an external loader; it does not implement Rustix's kernel services. The kernel requests protocol base revision 3, the higher-half direct-map (HHDM) offset, and the memory map.

Requests are kept in `.limine_requests_start`, `.limine_requests`, and `.limine_requests_end` by `linker.ld`. The response-bearing request records are mutable and the output `.limine_requests` section is placed in a writable load segment because Limine fills their response pointers before entering Rustix. The ELF entry symbol is `_start`.

### Entry sequence

1. Limine loads the ELF and transfers control to `_start` under the x86_64 Limine protocol.
2. `_start` configures the legacy COM1 UART for polling output and input.
3. The kernel disables maskable interrupts and installs its bootstrap GDT, TSS, and fatal-exception IDT. This does not initialize IRQ delivery.
4. The kernel copies the HHDM and memory-map responses into an owned `BootInfo` snapshot, including a frame allocator built only from validated usable ranges. It rejects malformed metadata before starting the shell.
5. The kernel reports validated ranges, frame counts, and baseline CPUID features, then seeds a volatile RAM filesystem and enters Crabshell on the serial console.
6. The shell busy-polls COM1 because no scheduler or UART interrupt handler exists yet. The kernel does not return to the loader.

The memory-map snapshot stores physical regions as checked half-open ranges `[start, end)` and retains Limine's known classifications plus unknown type values. It is diagnostic metadata only: it does not authorize Rustix to access every region, reclaim loader memory, or mutate the current page tables. The HHDM offset is validated and reported but is not yet used to translate or dereference physical addresses.

## Link and target configuration

- Rust target: `x86_64-unknown-none`
- Linker script: `linker.ld`
- Kernel virtual base: `0xffffffff80000000`
- Required code-generation constraints: kernel code model, static relocation, and disabled red zone
- Rust panic strategy: abort; the panic handler logs and halts

See [`../development/building.md`](../development/building.md) for commands and toolchain setup.

## Failure behavior and limitations

Missing responses, bad pointers/alignment, invalid HHDM values, excessive counts, null entries, address arithmetic overflow, and invalid or overlapping physical ranges reject the complete boot snapshot. `_start` halts before starting Crabshell rather than continuing with partial memory metadata. Structural checks cannot establish that a non-null loader pointer is mapped and readable; that remains an explicit trust assumption of the Limine handoff. The installed exception handlers print fatal context and halt; no fault recovery or maskable IRQ delivery is provided. COM1 writes use a bounded polling loop so a non-responsive UART does not block forever.

The repository includes a Limine v12.9.3 binary archive pin with SHA-256 verification, a hybrid ISO recipe, and a bounded QEMU serial smoke test that checks Crabshell's prompt. On 2026-10-16, `just verify` passed in WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 on the current working tree, and the QEMU log showed boot metadata before reaching the prompt. A clean-checkout run with uncached build/tool state and a CI run remain outstanding, so the baseline boot milestone is not yet complete. There is still no framebuffer console, reboot/shutdown interface, or broader boot-protocol compatibility test. The available serial and keyboard drivers do not imply a general device model.

## Future boot work

The kernel now snapshots and validates the Limine map and preserves firmware and loader-reclaimable classifications without reclaiming them. No region is considered Rustix-owned or free for allocation yet. Loader-reclaimable memory must remain unavailable until Rustix has copied any needed boot data and explicitly reaches a documented reclaim point; ACPI reclaimable memory needs the ACPI tables to be copied or parsed first. Frame allocation, page-table replacement, and ownership transfer remain future work.
